newsitem.title: USA: Mystery fumes again sicken dozens of Texas workers.
newsitem.headline: Mystery fumes again sicken dozens of Texas workers.

text.p: For a second straight day Wednesday, mysterious fumes smelling like cheap perfume swept through a Texas office tower, sending dozens of people to the hospital and forcing hundreds to evacuate.
Officials said 15 office workers with breathing problems, vomiting and dizziness were taken by ambulance to hospitals and another 15 were sent by bus for precautionary medical checks.
Thirty more, many of them sprawled on a grass bank and gasping for air, were given oxygen and treated by ambulance crews outside the nine-story Overton Centre office tower in southwest Fort Worth.

The fumes, which Tuesday hospitalized 72 workers and sickened 130 more, caused breathing problems and nausea again Wednesday morning just hours after fire officials concluded it was safe for workers to go back inside.
"It's the second verse of the same song," Lt. Kent Worley of the Fort Worth Fire Department said. "We've got exactly the same situation as (Tuesday) and we still don't know what is causing it."

After Wednesday's gas leak, the building's owners decided to shut it down until the fumes were identified and the problem fixed. By then, some of the 1,100 employees at the tower had said they would simply refuse to go back to work anyway.

A private company specialising in the so-called sick building syndrome was called in on Wednesday afternoon after the Fort Worth Fire Department's hazardous materials unit again failed to find the cause of the leak.
Fire officials said they believed the fumes may have come from the air-conditioning or heating systems but that they had been unable to find anything in several hours of tests.
None of the those hospitalized were believed to be in serious condition but Wednesday's leak caused panic inside the building.
Some workers said the fumes smelled like cheap perfume but others said they couldn't smell anything and were unaware of a problem until people around them began collapsing.
"As people were trying to make it to the bathroom, they started vomiting and some of them passed out," Stanley Harris said, as he stood outside with dozens of other employees.
